questions.stem: About oncotic pressure, the correct propositions are:
options: It is the term ωₚRT of the osmotic pressure Δπ = Δωᵢ·RT + ωₚ·RT
It is the osmotic pressure due to the diffusible ions
It expresses the ease with which proteins attract water
It always equals the total osmotic pressure Δπ, whatever the distribution of the diffusible ions
It is the osmotic pressure due to the proteins
questions.explanation: Oncotic pressure is ωₚRT, the osmotic pressure due to proteins; it expresses how easily proteins attract water. The total Δπ also contains Δωᵢ·RT from the diffusible ions, so the two are equal only when Δωᵢ = 0.

questions.stem: Two compartments are separated by a dialysis membrane; compartment (2) contains a protein of osmolarity ωₚ. At equilibrium ω₂ > ω₁. The correct propositions are:
options: ω₂ − ω₁ = Δωᵢ + ωₚ, where Δωᵢ = (ωᵢ)₂ − (ωᵢ)₁ is the difference of diffusible-ion osmolarities
If the diffusible ions had the same total osmolarity on both sides, Δπ would reduce to the oncotic pressure
questions.explanation: Water moves toward the higher total osmolarity: ω₂ > ω₁ ⇒ (1) → (2). ω₂ − ω₁ = [(ωᵢ)₂ + ωₚ] − (ωᵢ)₁ = Δωᵢ + ωₚ, so Δπ = Δωᵢ·RT + ωₚ·RT, which is ωₚRT only when Δωᵢ = 0.

questions.stem: A dialysis membrane separates two compartments of equal volume: (1) contains NaCl at 0.2 mol/l and (2) NaCl at 0.1 mol/l. At equilibrium:
options: The osmotic pressure between the two compartments is zero
The membrane potential V₁ − V₂ is zero
questions.explanation: Both ions cross the dialysis membrane, so each ends at C∞ = (C₁ + C₂)/2 = 0.15 mol/l on both sides (0.3 forgets to halve). With Δωᵢ = 0 and no protein, Δπ = 0, and C₁ = C₂ gives V₁ − V₂ = 0.
questions.mental: Equal volumes: just average, (0.2 + 0.1)/2 = 0.15 mol/l. Everything is the same on both sides, so Δπ and the potential are both zero, no calculation needed.

questions.stem: Across a dialysis membrane, an undissociated protein at concentration C is poured into (1) and a NaCl solution at concentration C′ into (2) (equal volumes). At equilibrium:
options: Δπ = CRT, with water flowing from (2) to (1)
To cancel the water flux, a pressure equal to CRT must be applied from (1) toward (2)
questions.explanation: The uncharged protein retains no ions: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ simply equalise at C′/2 on both sides, so Δωᵢ = 0 and Δπ = ωₚRT = CRT, water going (2) → (1). The counter-pressure CRT is applied in the opposite direction, (1) → (2).

questions.stem: Across a dialysis membrane, compartment (1) receives an undissociated protein at 2 mmol/l and compartment (2) NaCl at 100 mmol/l (equal volumes, T = 300 K, R = 8.31 SI). The pressure that must be applied to cancel the water flux at equilibrium is about:
questions.explanation: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are at 50 mmol/l on both sides, so Δωᵢ = 0 and Δπ = CRT = 2 mol/m³ × 8.31 × 300 ≈ 5 000 Pa. 254 kPa wrongly adds the salt; 5.0 Pa forgets that 1 mmol/l = 1 mol/m³.
questions.mental: RT at 300 K ≈ 8.31 × 300 ≈ 2 500 J/mol. 2 mmol/l = 2 mol/m³, so Δπ ≈ 2 × 2 500 = 5 000 Pa. The salt cancels out, which eliminates every option in the hundreds of kPa.

questions.stem: Across a dialysis membrane, a fully dissociated protein PrNa_z (concentration C) is poured into (1) and NaCl (concentration C′) into (2). The correct propositions are:
options: Each mole of Cl⁻ that crosses is accompanied by one mole of Na⁺ in the same direction
The proteinate Pr^z⁻ diffuses from (1) to (2)
At equilibrium, [Na⁺]₁ = zC + x and [Na⁺]₂ = C′ − x, x being the concentration of Cl⁻ that crossed
questions.explanation: Only Cl⁻ has a pure (2) → (1) gradient; n moles of Cl⁻ cross with n moles of Na⁺ (electroneutrality), giving [Cl⁻]₁ = x, [Na⁺]₁ = zC + x, [Na⁺]₂ = [Cl⁻]₂ = C′ − x. The protein cannot cross, and Cl⁻ stays unequal (x vs C′ − x): that is the Donnan effect.

questions.stem: In the same experiment (PrNa_z at C in (1), NaCl at C′ in (2), x = concentration of Cl⁻ that crossed into (1)), the osmotic pressure at equilibrium is:
questions.explanation: (ωᵢ)₁ = (zC + x) + x and (ωᵢ)₂ = 2(C′ − x), so Δωᵢ = zC − 2C′ + 4x; adding the oncotic term C gives A, and D is the same expression split into Δωᵢ·RT + ωₚRT. Option C forgets that x also leaves (2), and CRT alone ignores the unequal ions.

questions.stem: In a Donnan experiment, (1) contains PrNa₁₅ at C = 10 mmol/l and (2) NaCl at C′ = 150 mmol/l. At equilibrium x = 50 mmol/l of Cl⁻ has crossed into (1). The osmolarity difference ω₁ − ω₂ responsible for Δπ is:
questions.explanation: ω₁ = [Pr] + [Na⁺]₁ + [Cl⁻]₁ = 10 + (150 + 50) + 50 = 260; ω₂ = 2(150 − 50) = 200; difference 60 mosmol/l = zC − 2C′ + 4x + C. 10 is the oncotic part alone, which ignores the unequal ion distribution.
questions.mental: Fill the equilibrium table: (1) has 10 + 200 + 50 = 260, (2) has 100 + 100 = 200. Subtract: 60. Or plug into zC − 2C′ + 4x + C = 150 − 300 + 200 + 10.

questions.stem: The figure shows the membrane at equilibrium in a Donnan experiment (fully dissociated proteinate Pr^z⁻ in (1), NaCl in (2)) with the electric field E across it. The correct propositions are:
options: Compartment (1) is at the higher potential, since the field points toward it
The field points from (2) to (1), so V₂ > V₁
The face on the proteinate side (1) is negative
The potential difference is given by V₁ − V₂ = −(RT/zF)·ln(C₁/C₂) applied to a diffusible ion
questions.explanation: E points from the higher to the lower potential: (2) → (1) means V₂ > V₁, so V₁ − V₂ < 0 and the proteinate side is the negative face. The value comes from V₁ − V₂ = −(RT/zF)·ln(C₁/C₂) for Na⁺ or Cl⁻.

questions.stem: At Donnan equilibrium at 37 °C, [Na⁺]₁ = 200, [Cl⁻]₁ = 50, [Na⁺]₂ = [Cl⁻]₂ = 100 (mmol/l); the proteinate is in (1). The membrane potential V₁ − V₂ is about:
questions.explanation: For Na⁺: V₁ − V₂ = −(RT/F)·ln(200/100) = −26.7 × ln 2 ≈ −18.5 mV; Cl⁻ (z = −1) gives the same: −(RT/F)·ln(100/50). −8.0 mV uses log₁₀ instead of ln; a positive value contradicts the negative proteinate side.
questions.mental: RT/F ≈ 26.7 mV at 37 °C and ln 2 ≈ 0.69: 26.7 × 0.7 ≈ 18.7 → 18.5 mV. The protein side is negative, so the sign is minus; checking with Cl⁻ (ratio 100/50 = 2 again) confirms the value.

questions.stem: A voltage opposite to the membrane potential is applied to the Donnan system at equilibrium (PrNa_z at C in (1), NaCl at C′ in (2)). In the new equilibrium:
options: V₁ − V₂ = 0, so each diffusible ion has the same concentration on both sides
The proteinate becomes equally distributed between (1) and (2)
questions.explanation: With V₁ − V₂ = 0, −(RT/zF)·ln(C₁/C₂) = 0 ⇒ C₁ = C₂ for each diffusible ion: [Cl⁻] = (x + C′ − x)/2 = C′/2 and [Na⁺] = (zC + x + C′ − x)/2 = (zC + C′)/2. The protein still cannot cross.

questions.stem: Across a dialysis membrane, (1) contains PrNa_z at C, and (2) contains NaCl at C′ plus the same PrNa_z at the same concentration C. At equilibrium:
options: There is no Donnan effect, since [Pr^z⁻]₁ = [Pr^z⁻]₂
questions.explanation: With the same proteinate on both sides, the diffusible ions just equalise: Na⁺ averages zC and C′ + zC to (C′ + 2zC)/2, Cl⁻ averages to C′/2. C₁ = C₂ for every ion, so V₁ − V₂ = 0: no Donnan effect.

questions.stem: About osmotically active particles and Donnan equilibrium, the correct propositions are:
options: Across a semipermeable membrane, particles that cannot diffuse cause water to move and generate osmotic pressure
Particles that can cross the membrane are said to be osmotically active
In Donnan equilibrium, the diffusible ions keep diffusing indefinitely across the dialysis membrane
At Donnan equilibrium, only the non-diffusible protein contributes to the osmotic pressure
At Donnan equilibrium, the diffusible particles, together with the non-diffusible protein, contribute to the osmotic pressure
questions.explanation: Non-diffusible particles are the osmotically active ones across a semipermeable membrane. Across a dialysis membrane, diffusible particles diffuse until equilibrium, then stop, and together with the protein contribute to the osmotic pressure (Δπ = Δωᵢ·RT + ωₚRT).

questions.stem: About fluids and their flow, the correct propositions are:
options: A streamline is perpendicular to the velocity vector at every point
Flow is the overall motion of a fluid
A streamline is a curve that is tangent to the velocity vector at every point
questions.explanation: Fluids are liquids and gases; flow is their overall motion; a streamline is tangent (not perpendicular) to the velocity vector at every point.

questions.stem: About laminar flow, turbulent flow and viscosity, the correct propositions are:
options: In laminar flow, the streamlines are parallel
Turbulent flow occurs at high velocities and is disordered
Flow is laminar at high velocities
Viscosity is the resistance of a fluid to laminar flow
In turbulent flow, the streamlines are parallel
questions.explanation: Flow is laminar at low velocities (parallel streamlines) and turbulent at high velocities (disordered). Viscosity is the stickiness, the resistance to the laminar flow of a fluid.

questions.stem: About the viscosity coefficient η, the correct propositions are:
options: A real fluid has zero viscosity
η is expressed in poiseuille (Pl), with 1 Pl = 1 Pa·s
A perfect fluid has an infinite viscosity
questions.explanation: [η] = poiseuille, 1 Pl = 1 Pa·s (a product, not a quotient). A perfect fluid has η = 0; a real fluid has η ≠ 0.

questions.stem: A pump delivers 5 litres of liquid per minute. Its volumetric flow rate Q_V = dV/dt in SI units is about:
questions.explanation: Q_V = dV/dt in m³/s: 5 l = 5 × 10⁻³ m³ per 60 s ⇒ 8.3 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s. 8.3 × 10⁻² forgets the l → m³ conversion; 5 × 10⁻³ forgets the minute → second one.
questions.mental: 1 l = 10⁻³ m³ and 1 min = 60 s: 5/60 ≈ 0.083, times 10⁻³ gives 8.3 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s. Two conversions, so the answer must be far below 10⁻² — only options D and E are that small, and D (10⁻⁸) has one conversion too many.
